Title: Deloitte recognized as a Palo Alto Networks Diamond Innovator Partner
The AI Threat Horizon: Why Speed, Edge AI and Baselines Are Our Best Defense
Context: Detection alone was never enough to stop machine-speed threats, but the issue is even worse in the era of AI attacks
Full Text:
The New Reality of AI Attackers

AI-driven attacks are on the rise, transitioning from theoretical risks to real-world threats. Recent investigations reveal that criminals are using AI to accelerate attacks at scale. We have observed attackers leveraging AI agents to execute context-aware commands with real-time decision-making. In one campaign that we observed, a highly persistent threat actor utilizing AI generated 117 unique scripts across multiple languages and executed over 8,000 unique commands in just 12 days whereas normal attackers usually do dozens of commands with a few scripts for similar time periods.

The behavioral difference between human operators and AI agents is staggering. In one attack we observed, humans acted followed by an agentic AI attacker. In the first (human attacker) phase, time between commands averaged roughly 24 seconds. The hackers made typographical errors, repeated manual checks and demonstrated environment confusion. On the other hand, in the agentic phase of the attack, we observed flawless, zero-syntax-error commands with a median gap of just 1.4 seconds.

When an AI agent is instructed to execute aspects of an attack, it rapidly scans networks, attempts to escalate privileges and utilizes legitimate native tools to blend in. Because of AI’s machine-speed execution, our Mean Time To Respond (MTTR) metrics must improve considerably. Attack isolation and near real-time response are now critical mandates. If we wait hours to react, an AI agent can have already enumerated our cloud infrastructure and extracted or encrypted our data.

To effectively defend against AI-powered attacks, defenders must employ AI-powered tools. This should be done right where the attacks happen. Defenders should also strive to understand the behaviors that separate AI-based attacks from normal operations, whether fully autonomous or partially controlled by a human.

The Power of Edge AI and Layered Detection

To counter adversaries operating at automated speeds, defense must occur where the attack takes place. Leveraging AI on the edge, specifically on endpoints and Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFW), is a major strategic necessity. Edge-based AI can process telemetry instantly, making split-second decisions to terminate malicious web shell sessions or block active privilege escalation attempts locally.

Edge AI is also exceptionally fast. In our own product deployment, edge AI operated in milliseconds rather than taking minutes like agentic LLMs. It can function independently of cloud access or continuous network connectivity. This capabilities shift is crucial for several key reasons:

Even if an attack vector is used to temporarily disable network traffic to operate silently, local edge AI maintains detection coverage

It enables defenders to catch and isolate threats at the earliest possible stage

It safeguards sensitive corporate data locally without requiring telemetry or proprietary data to be transmitted to the cloud for analysis

The Defender’s Ultimate Advantage: Knowledge and Context

Despite their speed, agentic AI attackers have a foundational weakness that affects any attacker: They enter your environment without information. To operate, they must perform extensive reconnaissance, port sweeping and environment enumeration. This is where defenders hold the ultimate upper hand through comprehensive AI analytics.

Winning against machine-speed adversaries requires turning the advantage into real-time detection through automated data fusion and detection. By collecting telemetry across diverse network, endpoint, identity and cloud sources, normalization can map these distinct data streams into a single, cohesive schema. Advanced stitching can then merge related events across these disparate sensors into unified, context-rich stories rather than disconnected events.

Observing these integrated stories allows AI analytics engines to establish baselines of normal organizational behavior across the entire ecosystem. While establishing baselines has been longstanding best practice, AI analytics engines have made it easier for defenders to create these and keep them up to date.

Because threat actors lack this context, their automated attempts to rapidly map the terrain inevitably trigger detectors against established baselines, immediately exposing their presence across our detection layers.

Detection alone was never enough to stop machine-speed threats, but the issue is even worse in the era of AI attacks. Detecting an intrusion minutes after it begins still leaves defenders vulnerable if no immediate action is taken, and in those minutes an agentic AI attacker can cause significant damage to your organization. To truly close the loop against these attacks, organizations must combine real-time detection with automated response capabilities, enabling instant attack isolation and automated remediation before critical systems or data can be compromised.

The Basics Still Matter (But Require A New Approach)

While the sheer volume and speed of AI attacks can seem daunting, there is a positive takeaway: AI-empowered threat actors are not invisible, and their campaigns are entirely detectable. Every attack that we observed triggered alerts, and deep forensic investigations enabled us to reconstruct the attack lifecycles.

The cybersecurity basics still matter. The tools we have relied on as defenders in the past, including XDR solutions, network monitoring and active prevention rules, are still essential and relevant today. We do not need to throw away our playbooks; we simply need to use them differently. By utilizing our existing tools to automate isolation, leaning into AI on the edge for real-time response and trusting our baseline knowledge of our own environments, we are well-equipped to win against the next generation of threats. Crucially, unifying these tools into a cohesive SOC platform connects the dots across the enterprise — where vertical integration and correct platform usage ultimately drive vastly superior security outcomes.

If there’s one thing to take away from this, it is that Mean Time to Detect and Mean Time to Respond (MTTD and MTTR) are still king. But if we want to win these battles, detection and response times must drop to minutes, not hours.

To safeguard your organization against the unprecedented speed and adaptability of AI-driven threats, now is the time to evaluate your defense strategy. Ensure your enterprise is equipped with advanced detection and response capabilities, deploy robust security technologies across your endpoints, network, cloud and identity environments, and continuously refine their configurations to eliminate coverage gaps. Take action today to empower your security operation with the real-time visibility, automated response, and contextual intelligence needed to stay ahead of next-generation adversaries.

Title: NGINX HTTP/2 Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-123633
Context: Related Unit 42 Topics HTTP, DNS, Threat Detection Background While researching NGINX, I independently found the HTTP/2 connection-state defect now tracked as CVE-2026-123633
Full Text:
Executive Summary

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free vulnerability in NGINX HTTP/2 that may let an unauthenticated attacker cause a denial of service. In the CVE record, F5 says code execution may be possible when address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed.

CVE-2026-123633 affects NGINX servers that accept HTTP/2 client connections and proxy requests to a backend when free worker connections run low. A fragmented request can leave an active connection marked reusable. Under connection pressure, NGINX can close that connection and free memory the active request still uses.

F5's CVE record scores the issue 9.2 Critical under CVSS 4.0. The NGINX security advisories page labels the issue medium and lists versions 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 as affected. F5 credits memN0ps (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42) among the reporters.

NGINX 1.30.7 on the stable branch and 1.31.9 on the mainline branch contain the fix. F5 also lists affected NGINX Plus releases.

Administrators should review HTTP/2 reverse-proxy exposure and upgrade to a fixed NGINX release or a vendor package containing the CVE-2026-123633 fix.

Background

While researching NGINX, I independently found the HTTP/2 connection-state defect now tracked as CVE-2026-123633.

An unauthenticated client can send a fragmented HTTP/2 request that leaves an active connection marked as reusable. When the server resolves a hostname during the request and free connection slots run low, NGINX can reclaim that connection mid-request and free memory its DNS resolver is still using.

I reproduced the use-after-free with AddressSanitizer (ASan) on builds of unmodified NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 source. The NGINX security advisories page lists 1.19.7 through 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 through 1.31.8 as affected and 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 as fixed releases.

I reported the HTTP/2 use-after-free privately to F5. F5's CVE record scores it 9.2 Critical under CVSS 4.0 and 8.1 High under CVSS 3.1. The NGINX security advisories page labels it Medium.

In my ASan test on a Debian guest, ASan stopped NGINX at the first read from freed DNS lookup memory.

The resolver path in my test stems from the HTTP/2 connection bug tracked as CVE-2026-123633. CVE-2026-123634 is a separate DNS resolver vulnerability fixed in the same release.

I also found a memory disclosure vulnerability that leaked a libc pointer. I used the address to calculate the libc base and work around ASLR when chaining the disclosure with CVE-2026-123633. I reported this additional bug to F5 as a separate issue. From an attacker VM, I achieved pre-authentication remote code execution on a target VM as the non-root NGINX worker. The chain required a non-default NGINX configuration, and some attempts did not open a shell.

F5 assessed the memory disclosure as a behavior limited to a non-typical configuration and has not assigned it a CVE at the time of writing, so I am leaving out its details and the exploit steps.

How the Connection State Defect Works

NGINX marks a connection reusable when it can close that connection under pressure. Stream creation should clear the reusable mark once a request starts, but ngx_http_v2_create_stream() leaves it set in affected releases.

When a client sends only part of an HTTP/2 HEADERS frame header, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection reusable and returns early. The code below shows that decision:

The reusable mark lets NGINX reclaim connections stalled on partial frames before they exhaust the worker's slots.

The client then sends the remaining header bytes. ngx_http_v2_create_stream() builds a live stream and increments the active stream counter, but returns with the reusable mark still set:

The 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 fixes clear the reusable mark at stream creation with ngx_reusable_connection(h2c->connection, 0). Figure 1 shows the sequence in affected releases:

Reaching the Resolver Use-After-Free

The stale reusable mark lets NGINX reclaim a live connection when it needs a free slot. In my test, a request-time DNS lookup opened a new socket and triggered the drain.

My test used an HTTP/2 proxy route with a variable upstream. The variable evaluated to a hostname that was neither a literal IP address nor a configured upstream group, so NGINX looked it up during the request. The lookup also had to open a new resolver UDP socket.

The worker opens a new UDP socket only if it has none for the selected nameserver. Cached answers and in-flight lookups also skip the socket-allocation drain I tested.

Opening the DNS socket needs a connection slot, so ngx_get_connection() runs a drain check first. ngx_drain_connections() acts once free slots fall to one sixteenth of worker_connections or below while at least one reusable connection exists. The drain function then selects entries from the tail of the reusable queue, sets each connection's close flag, and calls its read handler:

c->close = 1; c->read->handler(c->read);

My test client closed its socket with zero linger after completing the frame, leaving NGINX with an active request on a reset connection. When connection pressure triggered the drain, the HTTP/2 read handler tried to send GOAWAY on that socket.

A successful write would have left the request running, but the write failed with Connection reset by peer, so NGINX finalized the connection and request. The ASan free stack passes through ngx_http_upstream_check_broken_connection().

Request cleanup reaches ngx_resolve_name_done(), which frees the resolver state while the original lookup still holds a pointer to it.

In ngx_resolve_name_locked(), the DNS send runs before timeout setup. The send can drain the connection and free ctx. When the send returns, timeout setup uses the stale pointer, as the code below shows:

ASan reported that NGINX read memory from a freed DNS lookup context. The free path ran through ngx_drain_connections(), ngx_http_v2_finalize_connection(), ngx_http_upstream_finalize_request() and ngx_resolve_name_done(). Source review showed that, if execution continues past the reported read, ngx_resolver_set_timeout() can also write ctx->event and ctx->ident through that stale pointer.

In the run where ASan reported the read, I split the 9-byte HEADERS frame header after 5 bytes. For the control, I sent the full frame header first and then the HPACK block. NGINX sent a DNS query and kept running. Figure 2 follows the calls from socket allocation to the use-after-free.

Test Setup and Limits

I ran the ASan test in an isolated Debian 13 guest. NGINX was built from official 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 source with Clang 19.1.7, HTTP/2, ASan and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. I sent the HTTP/2 requests over the guest's loopback interface.

For the 1.31.8 run, I set worker_connections to 16 and opened 13 filler connections that NGINX had not marked reusable. Table 1 shows the sanitizer results alongside the released-source review.

Limits

A source build includes the HTTP/2 module only when configured with --with-http_v2_module. Distribution packages commonly enable it.

The ASan evidence in this article comes from builds of 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 over loopback. The 1.31.8 test configuration set worker_connections to 16 instead of the documented default of 512, and ran NGINX with master_process off. The sanitizer aborted that single process. The public fix commit also names upstream connection setup as a drain trigger.

Two-VM Demonstration

The two-VM demonstration combined CVE-2026-123633 with the separate memory disclosure mentioned in the Background section. The target ran NGINX 1.31.8 with a root master and a www-data worker under a non-default configuration. Figure 3 records the running processes, version, loaded configuration path and listener.

The first attempt from the attacker VM recovered a libc address but did not open a shell; the second opened an interactive shell as www-data. Detection and Hunting

In the ASan test, NGINX logged a connection-drain warning before the sanitizer aborted the process. The warning can also appear under ordinary connection pressure, while a worker exit can have unrelated causes. A release build may keep running after reading freed memory. Table 3 lists investigation leads for HTTP/2 reverse proxies.

Signal

What I Saw in Testing

What to Check

Unexpected NGINX process exit

ASan aborted the single-process NGINX test after NGINX read freed memory.

Investigate unexpected worker exits in production near HTTP/2 requests and connection pressure. A worker exit on its own is weak evidence of exploitation.

Connection pressure with request-time DNS

NGINX logged "16 worker_connections are not enough, reusing connections" at warn level during the ASan test.

Correlate the warning with resolver traffic and connection pressure on routes that resolve at request time. The warning and DNS traffic can also occur under ordinary load.

Table 3. Signals to use in detection and hunting.

The warning in Table 3 is logged at most once per second per worker, so one line can cover several drain calls. Because NGINX defaults to the error log level (which omits warnings), configure error_log at the warn level (or a level that captures more detail, such as notice or info), then correlate the warning with traffic and worker state.

Exposure Review

CVE-2026-123633 describes a use-after-free in HTTP/2 reverse proxies that are running low on worker connections. The path I reproduced used a variable proxy_pass hostname, a configured resolver and a new UDP socket. F5's CVE description covers a broader set of HTTP/2 reverse proxies.

Check the running configuration. A master process can select another file with -c, so check its command line before assuming that the packaged path is the live one. The command nginx -T prints the on-disk configuration, which can still differ from what the running workers loaded.

I only tested proxy_pass. Operators should also review variable targets in:

grpc_pass

fastcgi_pass

uwsgi_pass

scgi_pass

For a matching route, check the running build and how close the worker gets to its connection limit. I tested one DNS socket route, but upstream connection setup also allocates through ngx_get_connection(), so static upstream routes still need review.

Mitigations

NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 fix the HTTP/2 issue. No workaround is listed in the CVE-2026-123633 record. If an upgrade must wait, the following changes could reduce exposure:

Where the service allows it, disable HTTP/2 on exposed listeners. Check every relevant listen ... http2 parameter and, on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, any http2 on; setting in the http or server context. Either setting can keep HTTP/2 enabled. Disabling HTTP/2 can break gRPC clients and may increase connection use if other traffic falls back to HTTP/1.1. If HTTP/2 stays enabled on other listeners, the extra HTTP/1.1 connections can push the same worker closer to its worker_connections limit.

Raising worker_connections gives the worker more headroom under the same traffic, but an attacker can still exhaust the extra slots and the connection-state bug remains.

Test each change before deployment. After upgrading, confirm the running worker uses a binary containing the CVE-2026-123633 fix. A configuration reload (nginx -s reload) keeps the old binary running in memory, so perform a full restart or live binary upgrade.

Conclusion

The defect starts when an HTTP/2 connection stays marked reusable after a request begins. In my test, opening a DNS socket under connection pressure drained that live connection and freed resolver state that the request still used. ASan reported that NGINX read memory after it had been freed.

Defenders should identify affected HTTP/2 reverse proxies, look for worker exits around connection pressure, and install a fixed NGINX release or vendor backport. My resolver test shows one way to reach the use-after-free. F5's description covers HTTP/2 reverse proxies more broadly.

Title: Recent Trends and Tactics of Agentic AI Attacks
Context: In a subset of analyzed attacks, the first phase featured manual reconnaissance and connectivity checks by human operators, with a median inter-command gap of 23
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Attackers are weaponizing autonomous AI agents in real-world campaigns, creating a risk that until recently has only been theoretical. Between July and September 2026, we identified and tracked more than 10 global campaigns in which different attackers deployed autonomous AI agents to enhance their attacks. These agentic AI attackers operated at machine speed, compressing the attack lifecycle from weeks or days into mere hours.

These campaigns targeted diverse sectors, including government, logistics, hospitality, manufacturing, agriculture and education. In every observed campaign the attackers gained their initial foothold through web shells that were deployed via vulnerable web applications.

The novelty of the observed agentic campaigns was not in their techniques, but in their speed and efficiency. Following the path of least resistance with familiar open-source tools and lightweight custom scripts, the AI-driven operators matched the tradecraft of proficient human attackers while operating at machine scale, at times executing hundreds of unique commands in just minutes.

However, using AI agents came at the expense of operational stealth. The agents left unmistakable behavioral fingerprints that revealed the involvement of non-human operators, including:

Structured machine-readable output formats

Adaptive exploit selection

Iterative refinement

Chain-of-thought reasoning comments that appeared in shell commands

This article details the real-world scenarios that we observed, organized by the tactical patterns that define how agentic AI is being weaponized today.

Background of Agentic Attacks

What Makes an Attack Agentic?

An agentic AI attacker is an autonomous AI system — usually a large language model (LLM) with tool-calling capabilities — that independently plans, executes and adapts attack sequences without continuous human guidance.remote

Unlike chatbots that respond to individual prompts, agentic AI systems operate in a loop: they observe their environment, reason about what to do next, take action and then observe the results to inform their next step.

How Agentic Attackers Are Changing the Threat Landscape

The weaponization of agentic AI represents an increased threat to security for several reasons:

Speed and scale: An agentic AI attacker operates at machine speed. In the campaigns we observed, AI agents executed hundreds of unique commands within minutes.

Lowered barrier to entry: Attackers can simply provide high-level guidance while the AI agent automates intricate technical phases. This includes complex actions such as compiling kernel exploits, navigating cross-platform lateral movement and systematically compromising cloud infrastructure.

Adaptive reasoning: Unlike script-based attacks that fail when they encounter unexpected conditions, agentic AI attackers employ reasoning to try alternative approaches when failures occur. We observed agents attempting five different privilege escalation techniques in sequence when earlier ones failed, compiling custom exploit code on-target when pre-built binaries didn’t work.

Cross-domain fluency: A single agentic AI attacker can operate across Linux, Windows, various cloud platforms, web applications, databases and network infrastructures. This breadth of expertise would typically require a team of specialists.

New challenges in threat attribution: Because AI agents generate unique, dynamic payloads on the fly without distinct behavioral fingerprints, attributing attacks to specific threat actors is increasingly difficult.

The Agentic AI Attack Cycle

Our analysis of more than 10 campaigns observed between July and September 2026 indicates that the most successful intrusions consistently combined human oversight with AI agents in a unified operational model:

Human sets the objective: The human operator identifies a target and provides initial access — typically a web shell on a vulnerable web application. In some cases, the human operator executes the first assessment of the target.

AI agent takes over: The AI agent autonomously performs further reconnaissance, credential harvesting, privilege escalation and lateral movement.

AI agent reports back: The AI agent structures its findings using machine-readable output formatting and periodically checks in with orchestration APIs.

Human makes strategic decisions: The human operator reviews the AI agent’s findings and directs high-level strategy. This may include instructing the agent to target the payment system or establish persistence.

AI agent executes: The AI agent carries out the human’s strategic directives with tactical autonomy.

Figure 1 shows the attack lifecycle.

Common Characteristics of Agentic AI Attacks

A comparative analysis of AI-assisted campaigns that we observed revealed several defining operational markers. These characteristics are strong indicators of an agentic attacker rather than a human operator:

The speed of the attack

Use of section headers

Overly descriptive comments

Command Execution Rate

One of the most pronounced characteristics of an attack performed by an AI operator is its ability to rapidly execute a high volume of commands.

In one attack we investigated, the AI attacker was active for only 140 minutes across two days. In this brief period of time, the attacker progressed from initial access via web shell, to performing reconnaissance and enumerating the victim’s cloud environment, website and databases. Throughout the attack, the AI agent executed about 800 unique commands at an inhuman pace.

In another campaign conducted over a 12-day period, the attacker executed more than 8,000 unique commands.

To understand the difference in operational speed between human and AI operators, we checked the median inter-command gap between two phases of the observed attacks. In a subset of analyzed attacks, the first phase featured manual reconnaissance and connectivity checks by human operators, with a median inter-command gap of 23.9 seconds.

In the second phase of the attack, the operation was passed to an agentic AI attacker. Once an AI operator took command, the median inter-command gap dropped to 1.4 seconds. Figure 2 shows the median inter-command gap difference between the two phases.

Headers and Delimiters

In every campaign that we observed, AI operators used section headers in shell commands and scripts, such as ===[Title]===. These headers help AI parse the results of the executed commands faster. In human-operated attacks such headers rarely appear, and are usually only seen when an attacker uses a pre-coded script.

Figure 3 shows an example of multiple commands executed by an AI operator, with section headers that separate the output of the commands.

Chain of Thought Comments

A common indicator of agentic AI-generated code is using “reasoning comments” embedded within technical scripts. In more than half of the observed campaigns, we identified multiple scripts containing conversational, step-by-step reasoning notes. These notes explained the logic of the AI operator’s script execution, as Figure 4 shows.

Operational Trends of Agentic AI Attacks in the Wild

In addition to the behavioral fingerprints distinguishing AI operators from human attackers, our investigation revealed consistent operational trends. Despite targeting diverse organizations, the agentic AI attackers followed a similar playbook:

Moving across platforms

Relying heavily on web shells for initial foothold and persistent C2

Adapting strategy in real time

Demonstrating explicit awareness of deployed security products

The following sections detail the trends that we observed across the different campaigns that we investigated.

Multi-Platform Attacks

Many observed attacks began on Linux web servers, but quickly spread to other platforms. Each campaign aimed to expand as widely as possible across the targeted network, regardless of platform or technology. This is an example of how AI agents continue to lower the barrier of entry for less-experienced operators. While a human attacker might take years to master each operating system (OS), agentic AI can seamlessly move between them and even compromise cloud infrastructure.

Cloud Platform Abuse

Our investigation found agentic AI attackers misusing cloud services across three major cloud providers. We assess that the exploitation was adaptive — the agent discovered the cloud platform and pivoted to platform-specific techniques without any pre-configuration.

In one campaign targeting a US-based hospitality and gaming company, upon discovering an AWS EC2 instance role, the AI agent attempted to steal credentials via the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS). When IMDSv1 was blocked, the agent immediately adapted and switched to IMDSv2 token acquisition, succeeding after multiple iterative attempts.

Once authenticated, the AI agent enumerated 20 AWS services across eight regions, exfiltrating information about the victim’s buckets, email service and secret management. The ability to enumerate is a basic part of bucket functionality, but in this case it was misused for malicious purposes. Additionally, upon discovering S3 bucket names in the configuration files, the agent immediately targeted payment and financial data paths.

This targeted pivot suggests that the human operator instructed the agent to prioritize high-value financial assets. Cortex XDR detected the agentic AI attacker spawning multiple processes enumerating the victim’s payment resources, as Figure 5 shows.

We assess that a human operator instructed the AI agent only to collect information in preparation for a more aggressive future takeover, as no harmful actions were taken. We observed the AI agent testing its ability to write into production cloud environments, immediately deleting test files and examining the bucket’s policy and Access Control List (ACL) to see if the bucket was publicly accessible or had exploitable policies.

Multi-OS Compromise

The AI agents also demonstrated an ability to operate across multiple operating systems within a single attack chain. In one observed campaign, an AI agent initially compromised a Linux server via a PHP web shell, and was able to pivot to a separate Windows IIS server with stolen SMB credentials. The rate of the lateral movement was incredibly fast: Within two minutes of identifying the Windows IIS server, the agent began deploying ASPX web shells over SMB. Over the next 26 minutes it pushed webshells to more than 40 locations across the server, rotating between five different webshell variants and uploading custom web.config files to enable script execution.

Adaptive and Strategic Attacks

One of the features that makes agentic AI attackers more powerful than older models and automations is an agent’s ability to adapt its strategy based on what it discovers.

In one campaign, we observed the AI agent demonstrate a particularly adaptive strategy: After exploiting the initial victim, the agent autonomously identified and attacked the victim’s IT vendor and sister organizations.

After gaining an initial foothold on the server, the AI agent uncovered the credentials for the vendor’s self-managed GitLab instance on the victim’s compromised web server. Pivoting immediately, the agent probed the vendor’s site, mapped infrastructure via WHOIS and tried to brute force access to the vendor’s GitLab instance, attempting a supply-chain attack across the vendor’s client base.

During a brute-force attempt, the agent used real names of marketing team members. This targeting suggests that the AI agent may have performed additional open-source intelligence (OSINT) gathering to identify specific employees. No vulnerability in GitLab was exploited; the credentials were exposed through the compromised third-party web server.

When the AI agent read the server’s NGINX virtual-host configurations, it identified over a dozen related sister-company entities on the same internal network. It then systematically probed each entity:

Harvesting CSRF tokens from login portals

Attempting credential reuse with passwords stolen from the primary target

Launching four iterative SQL injection scripts against the parent company’s admin panel

The agentic attacker takeover flow is shown in Figure 6.

Beyond strategic thinking, agentic AI attackers can escalate and tailor their attacks rapidly based on new information. This adaptiveness includes:

Quickly creating custom payloads

Pivoting to new attack vectors

Reacting swiftly to tool and script failures

In another case, we observed an agentic AI attacker execute a port sweep using a script named scan.sh. Just 21 seconds after the port sweep, the agent ran a second script named scan2.sh. The second script contained tailored recon commands that matched the exact technologies discovered on each port by the first script. Figure 7 shows the content of both scripts.

Web Shell-Based Intrusions

Across all analyzed campaigns, initial network access was achieved by deploying web shells on internet-facing web servers. This trend reflects a preference among human operators for leveraging web shells when orchestrating agentic AI operations. Web shells provide a straightforward approach to establishing initial footholds at scale during opportunistic attacks.

As an alternative to a web shell, an attacker could establish a foothold on a victim’s machine using a reverse shell, a remote access Trojan (RAT) or remote monitoring and management (RMM) software. However, those methods typically require more operational effort and resources to create and maintain.

In some cases, we observed that instead of relying on compiled implants to send commands, the AI agents independently dropped and utilized web shells. This provided the agents with ongoing code execution and persistence.

Dynamic Command Encoding

Given the extensive use of web shells as an initial foothold, secondary payloads were routinely obfuscated using Base64 encoding — a standard technique in web shell-based intrusions. Any attacker piping multi-line code through a web shell’s sh -c interface will encode it, to avoid breaking the code on shell metacharacters, quotes and special symbols. What distinguishes agentic AI attackers from human operators is not the encoding itself, but the volume, uniqueness and variety of encoded payloads they produce.

In a typical human-operated web shell intrusion, an attacker might deliver a handful of pre-written tools via Base64, which are reusable and often appear across multiple victims with identical hashes. However, in the agentic campaigns we investigated, the pattern was different: AI agents delivered 40-100 unique Base64-encoded payloads in a single attack session, each one tailored for the specific target’s assets. No two payloads were identical across victims and no payload matched any known tool signature.

Evasion Techniques and Security Awareness

While the high volume and fast rate of command execution make agentic AI attackers “noisy,” they demonstrated explicit awareness of deployed security products. Apart from attempting to evade sensors, agentic attackers are now actively probing their configuration, understanding the enforcement boundaries of detection tools and attempting to debug why a security tool blocked an action. This level of security-aware behavior was observed across multiple campaigns and represents a significant escalation from automated attacks that we have observed in the past.

EDR Path Exclusion

In one observed campaign, the AI agent deliberately excluded endpoint detection and response (EDR) directories from file discovery commands. The agent executed the same find command on six compromised endpoints, excluding three different security vendors, as seen in Figure 8.

Notably, the same agent also ran a separate security tool enumeration command, checking for the presence of 16 different security scanners (nmap, nessus, openvas, nikto, masscan, nuclei, lynis and others), mapping the defensive landscape before proceeding with its attack.

Direct EDR Reconnaissance

Our investigation revealed multiple cases where AI agents transitioned from simple evasion to active reconnaissance of installed security stacks. These agents methodically interrogated endpoint monitoring solutions to map their operational boundaries, as demonstrated in the following observed behaviors:

The AI agent attempted to enumerate and exfiltrate the endpoint’s security product local directory, specifically hunting for sensitive configuration data and stored credentials.

In a display of iterative debugging, the agent applied strace to the Microsoft Defender for Endpoint process (wdavdaemon), analyzing kernel-level system calls to reverse-engineer how the daemon monitors environment activity.

The Absence of Custom Tools and Malware

One of the most interesting outcomes from our campaign analysis was what we didn’t find. Although in the course of our investigation we extracted hundreds of unique script payloads, we did not recover a single compiled backdoor, custom C2 framework, DLL implant or shellcode loader.

In most cases, the AI agent’s entire custom arsenal consisted of relatively simple, single-use scripts like PHP web shells, PowerShell WMI backdoors or Python credential harvesters. This is a departure from the usual tooling profile of advanced attackers, who typically invest in compiled, persistent implants designed for long-term access.

Unlike these attackers, the observed agentic AI attackers generated purpose-built scripts on the fly, tailored to whatever they discovered at the same moment. Thus, instead of a single “one-size-fits-all” implant, the attacker’s progress within the victim’s network was achieved through smaller, single-step scripts. Cortex XDR detection demonstrates how the agentic AI attacker could generate and deploy different script types under the same process chain, as Figure 9 shows.

Reliance on Open-Source Tools and Exploits

Although we observed many cases of agentic AI attackers generating custom code on the fly, campaigns routinely incorporated existing, open-source tools before resorting to custom coding.

One recurring example is the Copy Fail exploit (CVE-2026-31431), a Linux kernel vulnerability that appeared across several organizations targeted in the observed campaigns. In three separate cases, the AI agent attempted to directly download the exploit from external sources — either via the exploit’s official GitHub repo, or from the exploit’s website.

In a different attack sequence, the AI agent first uploaded a pre-compiled PwnKit binary and tried multiple invocation methods. When that binary failed, the agent fetched a pre-compiled CVE-2024-1086 privilege escalation exploit. Only after exhausting both public binaries did the AI agent begin writing custom C source code on the target, iterating through compilers and linkers. When the compilation attempt also failed, the agent tried to rewrite the exploit logic in Python.

In another case that combined open-source tools with custom payloads, the AI agent followed a similar, but more layered approach. After failing to execute a precompiled CopyFail for local privilege escalation, it compiled the PwnKit exploit from source directly on the target. Subsequently, for network reconnaissance, the agent wrote a custom C network probe tool (charon_lite.c), and built custom Python spray scripts on top of it using the open-source paramiko library.

Operator Fingerprints in AI Agent-Enhanced Attacks

With the rise of AI agent-enhanced operations, fingerprinting operations with static payload signatures and behavioral tracking is becoming more difficult. We suggest alternative methods of fingerprinting agentic AI campaigns, relying on human intention, operational mishaps and infrastructure correlation.

During our research, we did not encounter behavioral markers that link agentic activity to specific LLM models or orchestration frameworks. While attack patterns like Base64 payload delivery and systematic reconnaissance commands are consistent, their implementations are too diverse to provide a unique behavioral fingerprint. Since AI-generated code is custom built for each target, signature-based attribution is largely ineffective.

However, it was clear that a human operator was behind these agentic infrastructures. A human decides which target to attack, when to launch the operation and which assets to compromise. Beyond operational intent, the human operators and their AI agents continue to leave behind key artifacts that provide crucial attribution leads:

Infrastructure

Hard-coded C2 addresses in payloads: In some cases, AI agents embed attacker-controlled IP addresses and network ranges directly into generated malware payloads and web shells. In one campaign, the C2 server 204.194.54[.]240 appeared in both PowerShell download cradles and cURL probes.

Agent orchestration infrastructure: Pivoting on the hard-coded 204.194.54[.]240 C2 server revealed that it was also hosting an instance of CyberStrikeAI, an AI-native offensive security platform. The presence of CyberStrikeAI allows us to pinpoint the use of a specific orchestration platform. This is the kind of infrastructure-level attribution that behavioral analysis alone cannot provide.

Cross-campaign infrastructure overlap: The malicious use of 204.194.54[.]240 is not an isolated incident. Recent threat research by ReliaQuest documented the same IP acting as a staging and reconnaissance node in a separate agent-driven attack. Their investigation also noted the presence of the CyberStrikeAI login page and open directories hosting privilege escalation tools on this address, corroborating the use of this specific infrastructure across multiple agentic campaigns.

Toolset

Accidental file paths from the attacker’s environment: In one campaign, we observed the accidental pasting of a local file path: /home/kali/exploitmasteryai/targets/warranty/shell5.php. The exploitmasteryai path fragment is the only concrete indicator of the AI attack framework’s identity across the entire campaign, and it was exposed purely through an operational security failure.

Linguistic artifacts leakage in code comments: Attackers interact with AI agents in a variety of languages, which results in code comments generated in those languages. Defenders can treat these as artifacts like native language comments in human-operated campaigns. In one example we encountered, the attackers used two identical versions of a WMI backdoor — one that contained comments in Chinese, and a newer version that was specified to be English only. Figure 10 shows both versions of the WMI backdoor.

Conclusion

Agentic AI attacks are no longer a theoretical concern, but an active threat targeting a broad range of industries. The campaigns we observed were aimed at government, logistics, manufacturing, hospitality, education and agriculture sectors. All of the attacks used the same method: A human operator points an AI agent at a vulnerable web application, and the agent takes it from there.

What we observed is not a new class of attack sophistication. The techniques themselves are the same ones that a skilled human attacker would employ. The agents follow well-established attack flows, rely on known CVEs and use the same open-source tools that human operators have used for years.

Where agentic AI attacks fundamentally differ is in their speed, volume and their ability to quickly and efficiently adapt to different types of platforms and operating systems. These feats allow agentic attackers to fully compromise a network in mere hours, where even an experienced attacker would take days or weeks.

However, in the attacks we witnessed, agentic attackers left behind unmistakable fingerprints that a human operator is unlikely to produce. These indications included chain-of-thought comments and specific content delimiters. Hunting for these signs could help defenders recognize and prevent this threat.

Ultimately, defending against agentic AI attacks requires AI-powered defenses, as these types of attacks are diverse, and require a solution that can identify patterns regardless of the specific tools, techniques or platforms involved.

Enforce multi-factor authentication

Enable sign-in rate limiting

Latest Insights

Emerging Activity Cluster CL-CRI-1264 (Vortex)

In September 2026, we identified a new activity cluster that we track as CL-CRI-1264. The tradecraft used by the attackers largely follows the wider playbook used by Com-affiliated threat actors, but a few traits set it apart. Most notably, we observed this activity primarily targeting healthcare, pharmaceutical and other medical organizations.

Attackers associated with CL-CRI-1264 establish initial access through vishing, where they pose as internal IT support and direct employees to servers using subdomains tailored to each targeted organization. These servers act as adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) proxies that pass user credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) approvals to the attackers in real time. Attackers have targeted employees on both their corporate workstations and personal mobile devices.

We have observed attackers behind CL-CRI-1264 enrolling an unauthorized MFA device within minutes of authenticating to establish persistence. In multiple instances, the attackers have reused a single device named Pixel 10a across compromised accounts. They have also automated data exfiltration using Python scripts (python-httpx User Agent) to target Microsoft 365 mailbox, OneDrive and SharePoint content.

Following exfiltration, the attackers have sent Microsoft Teams messages directly to employees at victim organizations, claiming data theft and directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site.

Emerging Activity Cluster CL-CRI-1274 (Cinder)

In September 2026, we identified another new activity cluster that we track as CL-CRI-1274. Similar to other activity detailed throughout this report, the attackers used vishing for initial access and avoided re-prompting for Duo MFA by replaying a persistent “keep me signed in” session token. They then replayed that same session token from proxy infrastructure.

From there, they used scripted access through python-requests (python-requests/2.34.2) and the Microsoft Graph software development kit (SDK) to collect and exfiltrate data from the victim’s SharePoint and OneDrive environments. Afterwards, the attackers used a compromised account to send extortion messages internally via email and Microsoft Teams, ultimately directing recipients to a Tor-hosted negotiation site.

Malicious Browser Extension

During an investigation attributed to another activity cluster, CL-CRI-1192 (which Google tracks under UNC6671), we identified a malicious browser extension (manifest version 1.6.111) named Google Chrome.

The extension was not on the Chrome Web Store. It was downloaded from an attacker-controlled server at oskeysetup[.]com and required the victim to manually sideload it using Developer Mode. Naming the extension Google Chrome helps disguise the browser's built-in warning banner (Google Chrome started debugging this browser) when the extension is active.

This domain's registration information closely resembles attacker infrastructure previously disclosed by Google and ReliaQuest in relation to the activity that we track as CL-CRI-1192.

This browser extension performs several malicious actions:

Installs global keyloggers

Steals local/session storage and IndexedDB data across all sites

Harvests authentication cookies (targeting Microsoft and Google accounts)

Scans pages for QR codes to capture login/MFA tokens

Streams webcam feeds

Furthermore, this browser extension implements a full command-and-control (C2) remote control module via Chrome DevTools Protocol (chrome.debugger). It allows operators to perform the following activities:

Capture hidden screenshots

Dispatch input events

Steal clipboard contents

Allow remote site navigation

We pivoted on this file and identified an additional browser extension also masquerading as Google Chrome (version 1.6.112) that communicates with the same C2 server. Both files share the same hard-coded API key.

We assess with moderate confidence that the attackers associated with CL-CRI-1192 developed this malicious browser extension as an alternative method to extract credentials from desktop and laptop devices running Chromium-based browsers such as Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge. The extension might also be shared with and used by other Com-affiliated attackers, although we currently have no evidence to suggest this.

We recognize Kevin Pham for his detailed investigation into this browser extension in a September 2026 write-up.

Victimology

Our telemetry shows sustained campaigns by Com-affiliated threat actors accelerating significantly around August 2026. The victims share a common profile: they hold large volumes of high-impact corporate data where exposure carries severe regulatory, legal or market consequences. Financial services, healthcare and legal organizations were primary targets, though activity spans across other industries.

Rather than targeting generic mailboxes, actors systematically sought individuals or systems responsible for high-value files, documents and databases. These attacks focused on:

Legal and corporate strategy: Actors targeted partner communications, firm strategy, executive compensation and pending contracts. They explicitly threatened to publish client agreements and confidential casework.

Financial and investment records: Attackers prioritized private investment portfolios, deal pipelines and large-scale cloud data warehouses. They occasionally exfiltrated tens of millions of customer relationship management (CRM) and recruiting records.

Healthcare and life sciences: Attackers targeted cloud data platforms containing patient records and proprietary research. To maximize pressure, actors broadcast extortion notices across internal chat channels and threatened regulatory reporting.

The most targeted organizations have distributed workforces, centralized single sign-on (SSO) and extensive cloud collaboration platforms. They are also predominantly based in English-speaking countries. We have observed actors repeatedly targeting the same organization, sometimes returning weeks after a failed attempt.

Who Is Being Targeted: Industries and Countries

Our monitoring of domains linked to Com-related activity showed that their targeting shifted from financial services to healthcare in early September 2026. Figure 1 shows that these attackers targeted financial services organizations about twice as often as healthcare organizations in August 2026, but healthcare overtook financial services in September, around when we first observed CL-CRI-1264 activity. Healthcare continued to be the most targeted industry in October 2026, alongside financial services. Attackers also frequently targeted construction, high technology and transportation and logistics organizations.

Figure 2 shows that between August and October 2026, most targeted organizations were based in the U.S. However, we observed increased targeting of Australian organizations beginning in late September 2026. Australian organizations made up less than 1% of observed subdomains in August and September, rising to about 13% in October. Organizations in Australia are now the second most targeted.

Tactics, Techniques and Procedures

Infrastructure and Tooling

A key characteristic of Com-affiliated threat actors is their use of apex domains that pose as SSO portals, IT support pages and passkey configuration services. These domains often host short-lived subdomains that impersonate target organizations, such as {company}.mfaregister[.]com. We actively track this infrastructure, conduct threat hunting for identified domains and publish key findings as Timely Threat Intelligence (TTI) in our GitHub repository.

Across Com-affiliated cases, we have identified similarities in hosting infrastructure, attack chains and victimology. In some cases, these actors also share tooling, such as Doko's Panel, an operator-controlled AiTM phishing kit.

As previously reported by Push Security, some Okta-targeting variants of the kit replace the panel's default backend.php handler with the renamed endpoint api_FyekIDWY.php. We observed this endpoint on multiple domains associated with Com-affiliated cases.

In at least one financial services case, telemetry recorded a full AiTM sequence from credential entry to an MFA number-match prompt, indicating a likely successful session capture, as shown in Figure 3.

Domains consistent with Com-affiliated infrastructure have also been observed in campaigns that use different techniques to target victims. For example, Microsoft reported oskeyregister[.]com in its research into passkey-themed social engineering.

Attacker Playbook

We did not observe a standard playbook employed by Com-affiliated threat actors. Rather than employing custom tools, the threat actors primarily leveraged native cloud utilities and selectively limited executions and persistence deployments.

Intrusions typically begin with vishing, in which threat actors pose as IT staff resolving an authentication issue and direct the victim to a phishing page tailored to their organization. After the AiTM kit captures credentials and session tokens, the attackers quickly enroll their own MFA devices, misuse cloud utilities and, in some cases, deploy malicious browser extensions to exfiltrate data and extort victims.

Using the harvested authentication data, Com-affiliated threat actors authenticate to victim environments, typically routing through residential proxy networks and commercial VPNs. They then seek to establish multi-layered persistence, enumerate sensitive data and exfiltrate data from cloud platforms. We observed the following techniques across Com-affiliated threat actors:

Persistence

Enrolling unauthorized MFA devices and workstation objects

Generating cloud infrastructure temporary credentials

Authorizing unapproved third-party OAuth applications or data-sync utilities

Staging secondary accounts or harvesting redundant credentials

Discovery and Defense Evasion

Monitoring authentications, permissions and mailboxes

Modifying calendar settings and mailbox rules

Clearing security alert events

Rotating infrastructure

Exfiltration

Using open-source tools such as Rclone and cloud storage platforms

Exfiltrating via native SaaS and REST APIs or scripted HTTP-based exfiltration

Moving data via SaaS to SaaS transfers

Conclusion

Earlier this year, our 2026 Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report found that extortion incidents in 2025 not using encryption (at 78%) dropped below the 90% range for the first time in several years. This trend has continued into 2026 and we don’t expect a slowdown. Title: Palo Alto Networks bets $4.5B on enterprise AI with Applied Compute acquisition
Context: Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings
Full Text:
Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion, a move the company said will let it train, deploy and secure open-weight AI models for enterprises in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments.

“The acquisition will bring Applied Compute’s platform and world-class AI research team to Palo Alto Networks to help enterprises adopt AI securely, whether they choose open-weight models, closed frontier models, or both,” the company said in a statement released alongside its fiscal first quarter 2027 results. The statement described Applied Compute as “a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models” and said the startup will continue to serve AI-native companies, digital natives and large enterprises.

The transaction is expected to close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027, which runs from February to April, the statement said. Applied Compute co-founder and CEO Yash Patil will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer, and the startup’s research team will help build AI models across the company’s offerings.

A security company that wants to run models

Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and CEO, said on the company’s earnings call that beyond building AI into its own security products, “we will help train and serve secure sovereign implementations of open-weight models to the enterprise.”

“Open-weight model implementations will allow us to deliver secure, open-weight models to our customers to enable adoption of secure AI in the enterprise,” Arora said. He said open-weight models had grown from under 5% of token traffic to more than 60% over the past year, without saying where the figure came from.

Asked by JP Morgan analyst Brian Essex about customer demand, Arora said deterministic security controls “cannot anticipate every scenario that an agent is going to conduct.” Enterprises building AI applications “will have to train a supervisory AI model at the same time,” he said, because Palo Alto cannot secure models it has no part in building.

“I cannot go in and intercept and understand somebody else’s application,” he said.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said Arora has a point, since a generic filter cannot know how a particular application is meant to behave. But most failures in AI applications happen at runtime, through prompts, tools, and permissions, whoever trained the model, he said. He noted that Palo Alto has sold model-agnostic protection through Prisma AIRS since 2025.

“A supervisor trained by the same hands as the system it supervises is a colleague, not a check,” Gogia said, adding that CIOs should make sure someone other than the trainer tests the result.

GPUs and data centers

To train and host those models, Palo Alto plans to build its own compute capacity, CFO Dipak Golechha said on the call. The spending “will mostly go to GPUs and servers,” with a smaller share for the facilities that house them, he said. Palo Alto will “continue to source from our cloud partners” and add dedicated capacity over time, Golechha said. Arora said the company aims for more than100 megawatts of compute in the next three to five years.

Gogia said Palo Alto has sovereignty credentials for security data, including customer-held keys and a European Cortex service governed by Deutsche Telekom. “None of that yet extends to GPUs,” he said, adding that a US-headquartered operator faces the same jurisdictional questions as the hyperscalers it rents capacity from.

“A sovereign hosting offer with no named region, operator or date is a promise looking for an address,” Gogia said. Compliance officers should ask Palo Alto for a region list, the operator, and a dated certification plan, he said.

Arora said on the call that the training and inference business could eventually exceed Palo Alto’s core market. “This could be bigger than what we do today,” he said.

One vendor, more of the stack

The deal follows Palo Alto’s $25 billion purchase of CyberArk, which added identity security to its platform. Gogia said Applied Compute would now add the models themselves to a supplier already at the center of many customers’ firewalls, SOC, and identity controls.

“Palo Alto is asking enterprises to let the guard build the vault it guards,” he said. One team watching both model and telemetry can spot trouble sooner, he said, but a single fault, breach or pricing dispute would land “on the protection and the protected together.”

CIOs should get a costed exit in writing before any model work moves across, Gogia said. Applied Compute customers should use the months before closing to secure ownership of trained weights in an exportable format, no training on their data without consent, a right to exit on change of control and price protection that survives bundling, he said. “Terms are cheapest to win while the suitor is still courting,” Gogia said.

Title: Borrowed Code, Real Consequences: What OPTIMJACK Teaches Us
Context: 16, 2026, a threat actor exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into customer accounts
Full Text:
Introduction

On Nov. 16, 2026, a threat actor exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform to inject malicious JavaScript into customer accounts. Nicknamed OPTIMJACK, this campaign delivered that code to visitors of at least 178 organizations' websites.

The tampered code was delivered directly from the vendor's legitimate content delivery network (CDN), under the vendor's own security certificate.

Enterprises invest heavily in hardening their core web infrastructure. A single compromised third-party tool can undermine that work. OPTIMJACK is a reminder that any vendor script with dynamic execution privileges on your site is part of your direct production code.

Threat actors know that third-party apps are the path of least resistance into lucrative environments. Defenders can respond with a fundamental principle that security engineering has relied on from the beginning: segmentation.

What Happened in OPTIMJACK

On Nov. 16th, 2026, the attacker exploited the vulnerability to place malicious JavaScript in the custom Project JavaScript field of customer accounts.

Because the tampered snippets were served from the vendor's legitimate CDN under its own certificate, at least 178 organizations, including well-known media, technology and financial services brands, unknowingly served the code to their visitors.

Once the code loaded in a visitor's browser, it did three things:

Cryptocurrency wallet swapping: It replaced wallet addresses that visitors copied with the attacker's own

Payment card skimming: It collected card details from checkout forms

Mobile exploit delivery: It attempted to deliver the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits to iPhones and iPads

Optimizely patched the flaw, removed the injected code and secured affected accounts early on November 17.

Trusted Vendors Are the Path of Least Resistance

Websites are not a single monolith. They are dynamic assemblies of dozens of third-party scripts, analytics tags and optimization tools.

That diversity drives speed, but it also introduces new vectors of attack through the software supply chain. When attackers compromise a single trusted vendor upstream, they bypass the perimeter defenses that vendor's customers have built.

The choice of malicious payload also matters. Swapping valid cryptocurrency wallet addresses on a page is a quick and persistent way to direct ill-gotten payments to a threat actor.

Segmentation Is the Strongest Step Available Today

If a third-party script executes on your page, it effectively has the same privileges as your own developers. Organizations need to architect their sites with that assumption in mind.

The best thing security teams can do right now is apply strict segmentation. The goal is simple— a compromised vendor script should never be able to touch sensitive user inputs. Methods of accomplishing this goal include:

Remove non-essential tags from sensitive pages: Strip all non-essential marketing, experimentation and analytics tags from authentication and checkout pages

Isolate payment collection: Place payment collection inside hardened, cross-origin iframes

Segmentation has been a cornerstone of good security engineering since the beginning.

What Affected Organizations Should Know

Even with the flaw patched, affected websites still need to act. Security teams should take these steps now:

Audit all project modifications made while the malicious code was available

Double-check all code that may have been altered during that period

Treat exposed payment data as potentially compromised, including payment card details entered into checkout forms on affected pages

Conclusion

OPTIMJACK is a reminder that any vendor script with dynamic execution privileges on your site is part of your direct production code. One vulnerability at a single vendor allowed an attacker to reach visitors of at least 178 organizations through a trusted, legitimate delivery channel.

Third-party scripts drive speed, but when they execute on your page, they effectively have the same privileges as your own developers.

Administrators of affected websites should start with the cleanup steps above. These segmentation steps will help keep a compromised vendor script away from sensitive user inputs. Isolating and segmenting as much as possible is key to software supply chain security management.

Full Text:
Executive Summary

Unit 42 has uncovered a multi-stage cyberespionage campaign that has been targeting Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025. We track this activity as TGR-STA-0049 (also tracked as REF7707, Earth Alux, Ink Dragon). The defining signature of the threat actor behind the activity is the targeting of government entities, combined with the use of advanced custom payloads that are designed for high-stealth intelligence collection operations, with an emphasis on evading security detection tools.

The campaign we investigated demonstrates high operational stealth and novel tool sets.

Activity associated with this group previously included deploying Squidoor (AKA FINALDRAFT) – an advanced backdoor used against high-value global targets since 2023.

Recently, activity associated with this group has included expanded tradecraft. Associated activity that we observed included deploying two previously undocumented custom remote access Trojans (RATs): PerfectPioneer RAT (spotted in July 2025) and its modular successor, KUKURAT (deployed in March 2026).

Over a nine-month period, we observed the attackers behind the activity consistently refining their capabilities to meet evolving operational needs. This campaign’s tradecraft features three particularly advanced capabilities:

Covert HTTP/3 (QUIC) C2 communications: An early adoption of HTTP/3 over UDP, providing a highly efficient command and control channel that may bypass traditional TCP-optimized deep packet inspection.

An operational safety switch: PerfectPioneer RAT features a built-in validation engine that actively blocks remote operators from executing noisy or destructive commands that could trigger environment security alerts.

Multi-vector heuristic camouflage: KUKURAT employs a custom spoofing engine that generates synthetic, benign-looking network, registry and file activity. By manipulating the behavioral baseline of the endpoint, it can successfully obscure indicators of compromise within a vast volume of artificial noise.

We provide a comprehensive technical breakdown of these unique malware families, the group’s evolving techniques, tactics and procedures (TTPs) and the highly targeted data exfiltration observed in this campaign.

Cortex AgentiX Agentic Assistant streamlined our investigation.
